name: DAILY fires later today while the time has not passed
DAILY rolls to tomorrow once the time has passed
WEEKLY fires later today while the time has not passed
WEEKLY rolls a full week once the time has passed
EVERY_N_DAYS lands on the anchored progression, not on today plus N
why: Anchored 2026-08-10 (epoch day 20675) every 3 days, asked on the 11th: the progression runs 10th, 13th, 16th, so the answer is the 13th and never the 14th.

name: EVERY_N_DAYS anchored today fires today while the time is still ahead
EVERY_N_DAYS anchored today skips a whole interval once the time has passed
why: A progression day that has already come round is spent; the next one is a full interval away, not tomorrow.

name: EVERY_N_DAYS with a future anchor waits for the anchor day itself
CONTESTED: the anchor progression around the evening cutoff
why: ReminderPlannerTest.everyNDaysUsesItsAnchorProgression asserted 2026-08-16 for this rule and had been failing on main for that reason. Anchor 20670 is 2026-08-05, so with an interval of 3 the progression runs 5th, 8th, 11th, 14th, 17th - the 16th is not on it, and no implementation could ever have returned it. Both sides compute the 14th at 20:00, which is after the 13th at 21:00, so nothing is bumped past a cutoff. The test was wrong and this case supersedes it.

name: a one-off on a future day is that day
a one-off today fires while its time is still ahead
CONTESTED: a one-off whose time passed earlier today has nothing left
why: Same decision as the elapsed one-off below, on the day it turns over.

name: CONTESTED: an elapsed one-off has no next occurrence
why: The TypeScript side returned the moment it fired and called it Next; the Java side returned null, and both suites passed. Null is the answer, because the question this function is asked is when the rule fires next, strictly after now - which is what every recurring branch already answers, and the one-off was the only carve-out. It had no caller acting on it either: the editor formatted the past moment under a Next: label, and the scheduler discarded it. The list row is where an elapsed one-off is still shown, and it reads the stored day rather than this function (vocabulary/reminderLabel.ts).

name: DST: a wall-clock time keeps its wall clock across the spring forward
why: Warsaw loses an hour at 02:00 on 2026-03-29. 08:00 stays 08:00 and the real gap to it is 23 hours, which is the whole reason the schema stores a rule and not a next-fire instant.

name: DST: a time inside the spring-forward gap moves forward by the gap
why: 02:30 does not exist on 2026-03-29. Both sides land on 03:30 rather than throwing or falling back a day - JavaScript because setHours rolls through the gap, Java because atZone shifts a gap local time later by its length. Recorded because it is agreement neither implementation states, not because anyone sets a reminder there on purpose.

name: DST: a time inside the ambiguous fall-back hour takes the earlier offset
why: 02:30 happens twice on 2026-10-25. Both sides take the first one, still on summer time.

name: DST: a wall-clock time keeps its wall clock across the fall back
a zone at a half-hour offset with no DST at all
a southern-hemisphere zone entering DST, so the rule is not Europe's
an anchored progression stepping across a southern-hemisphere DST shift
why: Anchor 2026-09-24 (epoch day 20720) every 3 days: the 27th is a progression day and also the day Auckland gains an hour.
